THOUGHT: The patient is a 19-year-old male with progressive, well-demarcated hypopigmented macules and patches on sun-exposed areas (face, hands, arms), no inflammation, scaling, pruritus, or systemic symptoms. Family history is notable — his father has a similar condition — suggesting a hereditary or autoimmune predisposition. Physical exam shows normal skin texture, no induration or erythema, and normal hair/nails. Crucially, the skin biopsy reveals *absence of melanocytes in the epidermis* with otherwise normal keratinocyte architecture and no fungal elements. This histopathologic finding is pathognomonic for *melanocyte loss*, not just reduced pigment production (e.g., as in pityriasis alba or tinea versicolor). Tinea versicolor would show hyphae/spores on KOH prep or biopsy and typically has fine scale; vitiligo does not. Post-inflammatory hypopigmentation would follow an antecedent inflammatory process (e.g., eczema, psoriasis), which is absent here. Albinism is congenital and generalized, not acquired and segmental/focal. The gradual onset, familial pattern (vitiligo has strong genetic associations, including autosomal dominant inheritance in some familial cases), and biopsy-confirmed melanocyte destruction all point decisively to vitiligo. The distribution (face, hands, arms) is consistent with the common “acral” and “facial” patterns of non-segmental vitiligo.

DIAGNOSIS: Vitiligo
